tweets.text: @edwardjhu congrats Edward! They are lucky to have you

Sharing some weekend reading. Faraday is a pretty interesting paper.

They train a 27B model to replicate results from AI research papers, with Codex available as a tool. The benchmark results are good, but a few things in the setup stood out more to me.

“Scientific taste” may actually be trainable. Faraday doesn’t seem to get better mainly by writing better code. It gets better at deciding what experiment to run, what evidence would actually support the claim, and when Codex has found a shortcut that produces the right-looking result for the wrong reason.

Their RL setup is also pretty interesting. There’s no clean unit test for “did good research.” They turn paper replication into something judgeable enough to train on, then use task-specific rubrics and turn-level credit assignment to learn which decisions in a long trajectory were actually useful.

It feels like a useful recipe for many long-horizon agent tasks where the reward can’t be perfectly verified, but good work can still be judged reliably enough.

The architecture is also kind of the reverse of what I expected. Most agent systems today put the biggest frontier model in the middle and have it route to tools, smaller models, etc.

Faraday’s 27B model is the researcher. Codex is a tool. The smaller model learns when to call Codex, what to ask it to do, whether the result is actually useful, and what to do next. The model with the most raw capability doesn’t have to be the one making the highest-level decisions.

This may have pretty important implications for enterprise agents too.

Maybe you don’t need to train a giant model to know everything about a company. You train a smaller model on how the company actually gets work done, what to delegate, what good looks like, which shortcuts aren’t acceptable, when to escalate. Then let it call whatever frontier model is best for execution.

tweets.text:
This feels like the end of the beginning for AI.

We’ve seen this movie before.
Electricity.
Bandwidth.
Cloud compute.

Infrastructure becomes abundant. Margins compress. Innovation moves up the stack.

Open models are making frontier intelligence increasingly abundant. That puts relentless economic pressure on the token business.

The next generation of great AI companies won’t be remembered for selling tokens. They’ll be remembered for building products people can’t imagine working without.

My bet: the next decade creates 100× more Harveys, Cursors, and OpenEvidences than frontier model labs. That’s where the next wave of value creation will come from. 

And these new generation of AI companies will own their models; the models will be the biggest differentiator of their products.
